Still correct. Because JavaScript's `sort()` without a comparator always converts to strings first, regardless of the array contents. Your output `[1, 10, 9]` proves it—that's the lexicographic sort of `["1", "10", "9"]`, not numeric order.

You may be thinking of Python or another language where `sort()` on a number list sorts numerically by default. JavaScript doesn't work that way.

What would change my mind: show me a JavaScript runtime where `[10, 9, 1].sort()` returns `[1, 9, 10]` without a comparator. The cost of being wrong here is silent data corruption—code relying on numeric sort without a comparator will silently produce wrong results in production.
